extracted.intended_audience: registrants' SEC reporting teams, corporate accountants, auditors, and advisors preparing SEC filings for business combinations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on performing the SEC 'income test' for significance in business combinations, including how to calculate pretax income and revenue components, treatment of step acquisitions, predecessor/successor periods, related businesses, and filing consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individually insignificant acquisitions: group separation and revenue component
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to separate the pool of individually insignificant acquirees into two groups – the group of acquired businesses with pretax income and the group of businesses with pretax losses. If the group with pretax income had material combined revenue (and the registrant had material revenue) for the last two fiscal years, the revenue component for this group is performed based on the group’s aggregate revenue. Similarly, if the group with pretax losses had material combined revenue (and the registrant had material revenue) for the last two fiscal years, the revenue component for this group is performed based on the group’s aggregate revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revenue component may apply to one group but not the other. If either group is significant at greater than 50% based on the lower of the results under the revenue component and the pretax income component (or just the pretax income component if a group does not have material combined revenue for the last two fiscal years), then the entire pool of individually insignificant acquired businesses is significant under the income test (not just the entities in the group that was greater than 50%). Example calculations in the guidance illustrate aggregation of revenues and computation of individual and group significance percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related businesses: combine revenue as a single business for revenue component
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple acquired businesses are related under S‑X Rule 3‑05(a)(3), the revenue of the related businesses are combined as if all related businesses were a single business for purposes of the revenue component of the income test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance for related businesses is not determined individually or by separating into pretax income and pretax loss groups. If the combined revenue for related businesses is not material for each of the last two years, the revenue component does not apply. See referenced Q&A for additional guidance on when businesses are related.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to calculate pretax income and revenue components (including step acquisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pretax income component is calculated as the relevant portion of the acquired business’s pretax income (for example, multiplied by the percentage interest being acquired in a step acquisition) divided by the registrant’s pretax income. The revenue component is calculated analogously using revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In step acquisitions, significance is measured relative to the additional interest acquired (e.g., if an additional 10% interest is acquired, perform the income test using 10% of the acquired business’s pretax income and revenue). Examples show: (acquired pretax income × percent acquired) ÷ registrant pretax income = pretax income component; (acquired revenue × percent acquired) ÷ registrant revenue = revenue component. The income test result uses the lower of the pretax income and revenue component results for significance determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude remeasurement gain/loss from pretax income component
rubrics_metrics.description: When an investor obtains control over an entity in which it holds an existing interest, it remeasures its previously held equity interest to acquisition‑date fair value and recognizes a remeasurement gain or loss in earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remeasurement gain or loss does not factor into the calculation of the pretax income component because it is not included in the registrant's operating results for the most recently completed fiscal year. (Thus exclude such gains/losses from the pretax income numerator when computing the income test.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance thresholds and filing consequences (20% and 50% rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance results drive disclosure/filing requirements. A level of significance above specified thresholds triggers different filing obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the greatest level of significance for the acquired business is less than or equal to 20%, filing audited annual and unaudited interim financial statements on a Form 8‑K is not required. However, pro forma financial information may still be required on Form 8‑K if the information giving effect to the acquisition would be material to investors (S‑X Rule 11‑01(a)(8)). Separately, for a pool of individually insignificant acquirees, if either pretax income or revenue group is significant at greater than 50% (measured using the lower of the revenue and pretax income component results, or pretax only where revenue is not material), the entire pool is significant under the income test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of successor basis or pro forma financial information in income test
rubrics_metrics.description: S‑X Rules 1‑02(w) and 11‑01(b) generally require use of the registrant’s historical financial statements for the most recently completed fiscal year to determine significance, but successor or pro forma information may be appropriate in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the registrant’s most recently filed fiscal year includes both predecessor‑ and successor‑basis financial statements (e.g., after a change in control or new basis of accounting), the SEC staff has indicated that the registrant’s successor period pretax income and revenue should be used for the income test. In other situations, with advance SEC staff permission (preclearance/CF‑OCA), registrants may use pro forma financial information giving effect to the change in basis as if it occurred at the beginning of the fiscal year. Examples show when successor or pro forma amounts were used and resulting significance percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment when acquired business’s most recent fiscal year includes successor and predecessor periods
rubrics_metrics.description: When an acquired business’s most recent fiscal year consists of predecessor and successor periods (due to a change in basis), the numerator used in the significance calculation depends on facts and timing of the split.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the successor period includes at least 12 months, use the successor‑only period. If the successor period is less than 12 months, the SEC staff generally expects pro forma financial information of the successor prepared for a 12‑month period (Article 11 pro forma) and does not permit simply adding predecessor and successor periods without pro forma adjustments. If the most recent annual period includes only predecessor results, use predecessor‑only information. Registrants may consult the SEC staff when results appear anomalous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using periods fewer than 12 months (change in fiscal year and other situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most recently filed audited financial statements covering fewer than 12 months may be used in limited situations: (1) registrant or acquired business changed its year‑end, (2) both changed year‑ends, (3) audited interim period financial statements were provided at underwriter/SEC request, or (4) the entity started operations fewer than 12 months prior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a change in fiscal year: if the transition period is fewer than nine months, the registrant may choose either the prior audited year-end statements or build a 12‑month period consisting of the audited transition period plus months from the prior audited year; if the transition period is nine months or more, the registrant must use the audited transition period (S‑X Rule 3‑06 equivalence). If both registrant and acquiree changed year‑ends, a consistent approach must be applied for both. Examples illustrate a six‑month transition period where registrant may use prior year or the transition period plus months to form 12 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use absolute value when registrant has a pretax loss in denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: When the registrant has a pretax loss in the period used for the income test, the absolute value of the registrant’s pretax loss is used as the denominator in the pretax income component calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show calculations where Company A’s pretax income or pro forma pretax loss is divided by the absolute value of the registrant’s pretax loss to compute the pretax income component (e.g., Company A’s pretax income ÷ |Registrant pretax loss| = significance percent). This approach ensures a meaningful percentage when the registrant reports a loss.
